senses.gloss: So complicated that it is hard to follow or to find your way through.
examples: The tax code is *labyrinthine*, even for accountants.
We got lost in the *labyrinthine* hallways of the old hospital.
Her novels have *labyrinthine* plots that reward a second reading.

position: both — the *with* sense usually follows a verb

senses.gloss: Mixed with a small amount of alcohol, a drug or something else strong.
examples: The punch was *laced* with rum.
Police said the pills were *laced* with fentanyl.
His apology was *laced* with sarcasm.

senses.gloss: Fastened or trimmed with laces.
examples: He pulled on a pair of heavy *laced* boots.
The dress has a *laced* back that ties at the waist.

senses.gloss: Without energy, care or interest in something that matters.
examples: The team's *lackadaisical* first half cost them the game.
He was let go for his *lackadaisical* attitude toward deadlines.
Nobody is *more lackadaisical* about answering email than my brother.

contrast: American spelling *lackluster*; the British form is *lacklustre*.

senses.gloss: Dull and without energy, excitement or quality.
examples: Sales have been *lackluster* since the spring.
Critics called the movie *lackluster*.
After a *lackluster* start, the band finally woke up.

contrast: *laconic* describes a person or a remark that uses very few words, often dryly. A short text that simply says everything briefly is *concise*.

senses.gloss: Using very few words.
examples: His *laconic* reply was just: Fine.
The sheriff was a tall, *laconic* man who nodded a lot.
She gets *more laconic* the angrier she is.

position: attributive only — *a lactating mother*; after a verb it is the verb: *She is lactating*

senses.gloss: Producing milk for a baby or a young animal.
examples: The drug is not recommended for pregnant or *lactating* women.
*Lactating* cows are milked twice a day.
The hospital has a quiet room for *lactating* mothers.

senses.gloss: Made of lace, or as delicate and full of small holes as lace.
examples: She wore a *lacy* white blouse.
Frost made a *lacy* pattern on the window.
The second dress was even *lacier* than the first.

position: both — before a noun it usually needs an adverb (*a heavily laden truck*); after a verb it takes *with*
form: an old participle of *lade*, to load; also the second half of compounds: *fat-laden*, *snow-laden*

senses.gloss: Loaded or filled with a large amount of something.
examples: The table was *laden* with food.
A heavily *laden* truck crawled up the hill.
His speech was *laden* with clichés.

contrast: The word now sounds old-fashioned, and *not very ladylike* is usually a criticism of a woman's behavior rather than a neutral description.

senses.gloss: Polite and graceful in the way people once expected a woman to be.
examples: She sat with her ankles crossed in a *ladylike* way.
Burping at the table is not very *ladylike*.
Her grandmother's idea of *ladylike* behavior died out long ago.

position: predicative only — after *be* or *get*: *He's laid up with the flu*
contrast: Do not confuse it with *laid off*, which means you lost your job because the company cut staff.

senses.gloss: Stuck in bed or at home because of illness or injury.
senses.ru: прикованный к постели, выбывший из строя
examples: He's been *laid up* with a bad back for two weeks.
I was *laid up* for a month after the surgery.
Half the team is *laid up* with the flu.

senses.gloss: Relaxed and not easily worried or made angry.
examples: Her dad is really *laid-back* about curfews.
It's a *laid-back* office — nobody wears a tie.
Portland felt *more laid-back* than New York.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the passive: *She was laid off in May*
contrast: *laid-off* means the job disappeared; *fired* means the person was let go for bad work or misconduct.

senses.gloss: Having lost a job because the employer cut staff.
examples: The city set up a job fair for *laid-off* factory workers.
*Laid-off* employees keep their health coverage for three months.
A group of *laid-off* engineers started their own company.

senses.gloss: Of a government or an economy: leaving business alone, with few rules.
examples: They argued for a *laissez-faire* approach to the internet.
The 1920s were a *laissez-faire* decade in American banking.

senses.gloss: Of a person: leaving others to do as they like.
examples: Her parents were *laissez-faire* about homework.
He has a *more laissez-faire* management style than his predecessor.

contrast: Used of a person, *lame* for unable to walk well now sounds offensive; people say *has trouble walking* or name the condition. The informal sense is the one you hear every day.

senses.gloss: Informal: weak, unconvincing or boring.
examples: That's the *lamest* excuse I've ever heard.
The party was kind of *lame*.
He made a *lame* joke about my haircut.

senses.gloss: Unable to walk normally because of an injured leg or foot.
examples: The horse went *lame* after the third race.
One of the puppies is *lame* in a back leg.

senses.gloss: Very bad or disappointing, in a way that deserves regret.
examples: The report describes a *lamentable* failure of oversight.
Her handwriting is *lamentable*.
It is *lamentable* that so few people voted.

senses.gloss: Surrounded by land, with no coast on the sea.
examples: Bolivia has been *landlocked* since 1884.
*Landlocked* countries pay more to ship their goods.
A dozen *landlocked* states depend on the river for trade.

senses.gloss: Planted and arranged to look attractive.
examples: The apartments have beautifully *landscaped* grounds.
A *landscaped* median runs down the middle of the boulevard.
The backyard is fully *landscaped*, so there is nothing left to do.

senses.gloss: Slow and relaxed, without energy, often in a pleasant way.
examples: They spent a *languid* afternoon by the pool.
She waved a *languid* hand at the waiter.
The music had a *languid*, sleepy rhythm.

senses.gloss: Tall and thin, with long arms and legs.
examples: A *lanky* teenager answered the door.
He's *lanky* like his father.
The *lankiest* kid on the team plays center.

contrast: Also a noun: *a Laotian*. The language is *Lao*, and *Lao* also works as the adjective.

senses.gloss: From Laos, or connected with Laos.
examples: We ate at a *Laotian* restaurant downtown.
Her grandparents are *Laotian*.
The museum has a room of *Laotian* textiles.

senses.gloss: No longer practicing the religion you were raised in.
examples: He calls himself a *lapsed* Catholic.
A *lapsed* Baptist, she still knows every hymn by heart.

senses.gloss: No longer valid because it was not renewed or paid for.
examples: The company sent a notice about her *lapsed* policy.
You can restore a *lapsed* membership for a small fee.

senses.gloss: Of a company or its stock: with a very large total market value.
examples: The fund holds mostly *large-cap* stocks.
*Large-cap* companies fell less than the rest of the market.
He moved his savings into a *large-cap* index fund.

comparison: not gradable — though the compound *larger-scale* is common

senses.gloss: Involving a lot of people, money, space or effort.
examples: The city is planning *large-scale* repairs to the water system.
*Large-scale* farming needs heavy machinery.
There has been no *large-scale* violence since the election.

senses.gloss: More colorful, exciting or exaggerated than ordinary people.
examples: Her father was a *larger-than-life* character who knew everyone in town.
The coach's personality is *larger-than-life*.

senses.gloss: Bigger than the real thing.
examples: A *larger-than-life* statue of the founder stands in the lobby.
The mural shows him *larger-than-life*, twenty feet tall.

senses.gloss: Showing open and offensive sexual interest.
examples: He was fired for *lascivious* comments about a coworker.
The town council covered the statue up because they thought it *lascivious*.
She caught his *lascivious* grin in the mirror.

form: compound — from defending the last ditch of a fortification

senses.gloss: Made as a final attempt after everything else has failed.
examples: The governor made a *last-ditch* effort to save the plant.
In a *last-ditch* attempt to pass the class, he took the makeup exam.
*Last-ditch* talks broke down after midnight.

senses.gloss: Finishing at the bottom of a competition or a ranking.
examples: The *last-place* team gets the first pick in the draft.
He went from a *last-place* finish to the podium in one season.
Their *last-place* showing in the polls surprised no one.

senses.gloss: Continuing for a long time, often for good.
examples: The trip made a *lasting* impression on her.
After ten years of war they finally reached a *lasting* peace.
Kindness leaves a *more lasting* mark than money does.

contrast: *latent* is present but not showing yet; *hidden* is something deliberately kept out of sight.

senses.gloss: Present but not yet active, visible or developed.
examples: The virus can stay *latent* for years.
Good teachers find *latent* talent.
The crisis exposed *latent* tensions in the coalition.

senses.gloss: At, from or toward the side.
examples: The knee has very little *lateral* movement.
A *lateral* line of sensors runs along the fish's body.

senses.gloss: Of a job change: to a similar level, not a promotion.
examples: He made a *lateral* move to another department.
The new title looks better, but it's really a *lateral* step.

contrast: Usually written without the hyphen before a noun: *Latin American literature*. The hyphen survives mostly in older writing and in phrases like *Latin-American relations*.

senses.gloss: From the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries of Central and South America, or connected with them.
examples: She teaches *Latin-American* history.
The festival shows *Latin-American* films all week.
Most of the players on the roster are *Latin-American*.

contrast: Also a noun: *a Latino*, *Latinos*; the feminine is *Latina*, and *Latinx* is a newer gender-neutral form. *Hispanic* points to the Spanish language, *Latino* to Latin America — Brazilians are *Latino* but not *Hispanic*.

senses.gloss: Of people in the United States whose families come from Latin America.
examples: The district has a large *Latino* population.
She is the first *Latino* mayor in the city's history.
*Latino* voters split almost evenly in the last election.

senses.gloss: Modern, or a modern version of someone or something from the past.
examples: He styles himself a *latter-day* Robin Hood.
The band is a *latter-day* version of the 1970s original.
It's a *latter-day* gold rush, with data instead of gold.

contrast: Also a noun — a person (*a Latvian*) and the language (*She speaks Latvian*).

senses.gloss: From Latvia, or connected with Latvia.
examples: She sings in a *Latvian* choir.
The *Latvian* team took bronze.
His grandparents are *Latvian*.

senses.gloss: Deserving praise, even if it does not succeed.
examples: The program has a *laudable* goal and a tiny budget.
Her effort to learn Japanese in a year was *laudable*.
It is *laudable* that the company published the numbers at all.

contrast: *laughable* means so bad or silly that people laugh at it. Something funny on purpose is *funny* or *hilarious*.

senses.gloss: So poor, small or absurd that it cannot be taken seriously.
examples: The offer was *laughable* — half of what the house is worth.
Their security was *laughable*; the back door was propped open.
He made a *laughable* attempt at an Irish accent.

contrast: Also a noun — the plant and its scent: *a field of lavender*, *lavender soap*.

senses.gloss: Of a pale purple color, like the flower.
examples: She painted the bedroom *lavender*.
He wore a *lavender* tie to the wedding.
The sky turned *lavender* just after sunset.

senses.gloss: Very large, expensive or generous in amount.
examples: They threw a *lavish* wedding for four hundred guests.
The reviews were *lavish*.
The director's *lavish* sets cost more than the cast.

senses.gloss: Giving a great deal of something, often too much.
examples: Her boss is *lavish* with compliments and stingy with raises.
Critics were *lavish* in their praise of the album.

form: compound — noun + participle, from *abide by the law*

senses.gloss: Obeying the law.
examples: He described himself as a *law-abiding* citizen.
Most gun owners in the county are *law-abiding*.
It's a quiet, *law-abiding* neighborhood.

contrast: *lawful* and *legal* overlap, but *lawful* sounds formal and is fixed in phrases like *lawful permanent resident*, *a lawful order*, *his lawful wife*.

senses.gloss: Allowed or recognized by law.
examples: Officers may use force only for a *lawful* purpose.
She is a *lawful* permanent resident.
The judge ruled that the strike was *lawful*.

senses.gloss: Without law and order, or ignoring the law.
examples: The border towns were *lawless* for a decade.
*Lawless* gangs controlled the port.
The internet is less *lawless* than it was in 1995.

comparison: -er/-est or more/most — *laxer* or *more lax*, *laxest* or *most lax*

senses.gloss: Not strict or careful enough.
examples: Security at the airport was *lax*.
The school has been *lax* about enforcing the dress code.
Standards got *more lax* every year.

contrast: Three other words look the same: the verb *lay* (*lay the book down*), the past of *lie* (*He lay on the couch*), and the noun in *the lay of the land*. The adjective lives in *a lay person*, *the lay reader*, *a lay preacher*.

senses.gloss: Not a member of the clergy.
examples: *Lay* volunteers run most of the parish programs.
A *lay* preacher led the service that Sunday.

senses.gloss: Not trained in a particular profession; ordinary.
examples: The book explains the science for a *lay* reader.
To a *lay* audience the two diseases look the same.

senses.gloss: Made or arranged in layers.
examples: Dress in *layered* clothing — it gets cold at night.
She got her hair cut short and *layered*.

senses.gloss: Having several levels of meaning or detail.
examples: It's a *layered* performance that gets better on a second viewing.
The report gives a *more layered* picture than the headlines did.

contrast: The *lead* here is the metal, and it rhymes with *bed*, not with *need*.

senses.gloss: Containing no lead.
examples: All the paint in the house is *lead-free*.
*Lead-free* solder is standard in electronics now.
The school replaced the old fountains with *lead-free* ones.

ru: содержащий свинец; со свинцовым переплётом (о стекле)
contrast: Two syllables, LED-id. *Leaded* gasoline was banned for cars in the United States in 1996; the word survives in *leaded glass* and in *unleaded*.

senses.gloss: Containing lead as an additive.
examples: *Leaded* gasoline is still sold for some small airplanes.
Old pipes and *leaded* paint are the usual sources of the metal.

senses.gloss: Of glass or windows: set in strips of lead.
examples: The church has beautiful *leaded* windows.
A *leaded* glass door separates the two rooms.

senses.gloss: Dull gray, the color of lead.
examples: A *leaden* sky hung over the city all week.
The sea was flat and *leaden*.

senses.gloss: Heavy, slow and without life.
examples: By mile twenty my legs felt *leaden*.
The dialogue is *leaden* and the jokes fall flat.

senses.gloss: Most important, most successful, or in first place.
examples: She is the country's *leading* expert on bats.
The company is a *leading* maker of batteries.
He played the *leading* role in two Broadway shows.

senses.gloss: Of a question: worded so that it pushes someone toward a particular answer.
examples: The judge ruled that the question was *leading*.
Avoid *leading* questions when you write a survey.

senses.gloss: Full of leaves or trees.
examples: They live on a *leafy* street near the park.
The trail is cool and *leafy* even in July.
The *leafiest* neighborhoods are noticeably cooler in summer.

senses.gloss: Of a vegetable: with large green leaves that you eat.
examples: Eat more dark *leafy* greens.
Spinach and other *leafy* vegetables are high in iron.

senses.gloss: Letting liquid or gas escape through a hole or a crack.
examples: A *leaky* faucet can waste gallons a day.
The roof is *leaky* in two places.
This is the *leakiest* tent we have ever owned.

senses.gloss: Of an organization: letting secret information get out.
examples: The agency has a *leaky* front office.
It's a *leaky* administration — everything ends up in the papers.

contrast: The verb *lean* (*lean against the wall*) sounds exactly the same but is a different word.

senses.gloss: Thin in a healthy, muscular way.
examples: He's tall and *lean*, like a runner.
Six months of training left her *leaner* and faster.

senses.gloss: Of meat: with very little fat.
examples: Use *lean* ground beef for the chili.
The recipe calls for a *lean* cut of pork.

senses.gloss: Of a period of time: with little money, food or success.
examples: The restaurant survived some *lean* years.
Farmers put something aside for the *lean* months.

senses.gloss: Of a company or a system: using no more people or money than it needs.
examples: The startup stayed *lean* — eleven people and no office.
They run a *lean* operation with two shifts and no managers.

position: both — the erudite sense goes before a noun (*a learned professor*); the acquired sense also follows a verb: *That fear is learned*
contrast: Two pronunciations. The adjective meaning full of learning has two syllables, LUR-nid. *learned* meaning gained by learning (*learned behavior*) has one syllable, LURND, like the past tense of *learn*.

senses.gloss: Having or showing deep knowledge gained from long study.
examples: He gave a *learned* lecture on Roman law.
The article appeared in a *learned* journal.

senses.gloss: Gained through experience or teaching rather than born in you.
examples: Fear of snakes is partly *learned* behavior.
An accent is *learned*, not inherited.

contrast: The noun has the same form in the singular and the plural: *a Lebanese*, *the Lebanese*.

senses.gloss: From Lebanon, or connected with Lebanon.
examples: We had *Lebanese* food — hummus, kibbeh and plenty of bread.
Her mother is *Lebanese*.
The *Lebanese* pound has lost most of its value.

senses.gloss: Showing unpleasant, obvious sexual interest in other people.
examples: Her boss was a *lecherous* old man who always stood too close.
He gave the waitress a *lecherous* look.
The character is funny, *lecherous* and completely unreliable.

position: predicative only — *I'm leery of cheap flights*

senses.gloss: Careful and a little suspicious about something.
examples: I'm *leery* of anything that promises fast money.
Investors are *leery* after last year's crash.
She was *leery* about lending him the car.

position: attributive only — for the side itself English uses the noun: *on the left*
contrast: Three other *left*s: the noun (*take the next left*), the adverb (*turn left*), and the past participle of *leave* — *There's no milk left* means none is remaining.

senses.gloss: On the side of your body where your heart is, or on that side of something.
examples: He broke his *left* wrist.
Take the *left* lane after the bridge.
The *left* side of the building gets all the afternoon sun.

contrast: *left-hand* describes where a thing is (*the left-hand column*); *left-handed* describes a person who writes with the left hand.

senses.gloss: On or toward the left side.
examples: The totals are in the *left-hand* column.
Take the *left-hand* fork in the trail.
The spare key is in the *left-hand* drawer.

contrast: American spelling *left-of-center*; British writing has *left-of-centre*.

senses.gloss: Slightly to the political left, but not extreme.
examples: The paper's editorials are *left-of-center*.
She won as a *left-of-center* candidate in a conservative district.
The government is a coalition of two *left-of-center* parties.

senses.gloss: Supporting socialist or strongly progressive politics.
examples: The bill was written by the party's *left-wing* members.
His views got *more left-wing* after college.
She writes for a *left-wing* magazine.

contrast: Also a noun: *a leftist*. In American English it often sounds disapproving; *progressive* and *liberal* are the neutral words.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or supporting the political left.
examples: A *leftist* coalition won the election.
The magazine has a *leftist* editorial line.
Her politics were *leftist* long before it was fashionable.

contrast: As a noun it is usually plural: *We ate leftovers all week.*

senses.gloss: Remaining after the rest has been used or eaten.
examples: We made soup with the *leftover* turkey.
There's *leftover* paint in the garage.
She used *leftover* fabric to make a pillow.

takes: *to*-infinitive in *it is legal to do something*
contrast: There is no *unlegal*: the opposite of the allowed sense is *illegal*.

senses.gloss: Connected with the law.
examples: You should get *legal* advice before you sign.
The company's *legal* department is on the fourth floor.

senses.gloss: Allowed by law.
examples: It is *legal* to turn right on red in most states.
Marijuana is *legal* here for adults over 21.

senses.gloss: Very famous and much admired.
examples: She was a *legendary* jazz singer.
His patience with beginners is *legendary*.

senses.gloss: Coming from an old story, and possibly not real.
examples: The *legendary* founder of the city was raised by wolves.
They went looking for the *legendary* lost mine.

senses.gloss: Having long legs.
examples: A *leggy* colt followed the mare around the field.
She was the *leggiest* girl in the class by sixth grade.

senses.gloss: Of a plant: tall, thin and weak from too little light.
examples: The seedlings got *leggy* on the windowsill.
Pinch the tops back or the basil will go *leggy*.

contrast: *legible* is about handwriting or print you can make out; *readable* is about writing that is easy or enjoyable to follow.

senses.gloss: Clear enough to read.
examples: His signature is barely *legible*.
Print in black ink so the form stays *legible*.
The inscription is still *legible* after two hundred years.

contrast: One of the three branches of American government: *legislative*, *executive*, *judicial*.

senses.gloss: Connected with making laws, or with the body that makes them.
examples: The bill died in the last *legislative* session.
Congress holds the *legislative* power.
She handles *legislative* affairs for a trade group.

contrast: The verb is spelled the same but said lih-JIT-uh-mayt, and the everyday verb is *legitimize*.

senses.gloss: Fair and reasonable; resting on good grounds.
examples: That's a *legitimate* question.
Parents have a *legitimate* interest in what is taught.

senses.gloss: Allowed by law or by the rules; genuine.
examples: The money came from a *legitimate* business.
Is this a *legitimate* website or a scam?

senses.gloss: Born to parents who are married to each other.
examples: Under the old law only *legitimate* children could inherit.
The court upheld the marriage and declared the children *legitimate*.

contrast: Far more common as an adverb: *Cut the zucchini lengthwise.* Before a noun it is an adjective: *a lengthwise cut*. *Lengthways* means the same and sounds British.

senses.gloss: Running along the length of something rather than across it.
examples: Make one *lengthwise* cut down the middle of the dough.
The table has a *lengthwise* groove for the cables.
A *lengthwise* stripe makes the room look longer.

contrast: *lengthy* usually carries a complaint: a *lengthy* speech is one you wished were shorter. For neutral length use *long*.

senses.gloss: Lasting or taking a long time, often longer than you want.
examples: The approval process is *lengthy*.
After a *lengthy* delay, the flight finally boarded.
The second hearing was *lengthier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Less strict or less severe than expected, especially in punishing.
examples: The judge was *lenient* because it was a first offense.
Our coach is *lenient* with freshmen.
Critics called the fine far too *lenient*.

contrast: Also a noun: *She is a lesbian.* As an adjective it describes people, couples and communities: *a lesbian couple*, *lesbian writers*.

senses.gloss: Of women who are sexually attracted to women.
examples: They were the first *lesbian* couple married in the county.
The novel has a *lesbian* main character.
She writes about *lesbian* life in the 1950s.

comparison: irregular — *lesser* is itself the comparative of *little*; the superlative is *least*
contrast: *lesser* is already a comparative, so never *more lesser*. It goes before a noun; after a verb use *less* or *smaller*.

senses.gloss: Smaller in size, amount or importance.
examples: He pleaded guilty to a *lesser* charge.
It's the *lesser* of two evils.
The same rule applies, to a *lesser* degree, to part-time staff.

senses.gloss: Less well known or less important than others of the same kind.
examples: The show includes a few *lesser* painters of the period.
Even his *lesser* novels are worth reading.

senses.gloss: Able to cause death.
examples: The snake's bite is *lethal* without treatment.
They gave him a *lethal* dose by mistake.
This strain is *more lethal* than the one from last winter.

senses.gloss: Very effective and dangerous to an opponent.
examples: Her serve is *lethal*.
The two of them together are a *lethal* combination on the ice.

senses.gloss: Without energy; slow and sleepy.
examples: The medicine made him *lethargic* all afternoon.
The puppy was *lethargic* and wouldn't eat, so we called the vet.
By August the heat makes everyone *lethargic*.

contrast: Also a noun (*the top level*) and a verb (*level the ground*, *level with me*).

senses.gloss: Flat and even, with no part higher than another.
examples: Make sure the shelf is *level* before you screw it in.
Set the tent up on *level* ground.

senses.gloss: At the same height or the same score as something else.
examples: The water was *level* with the top of the dock.
The teams were *level* at halftime.

senses.gloss: Calm and steady.
examples: She answered in a *level* voice.
He looked at me with a *level* gaze and said nothing.

senses.gloss: Calm and sensible, especially when things go wrong.
examples: We need someone *level-headed* running the meeting.
She stayed *level-headed* while everyone else panicked.
He's the *most level-headed* person on the crew.

senses.gloss: Sexual in a crude, offensive way.
examples: He was arrested for *lewd* behavior in public.
The song's *lewd* lyrics kept it off the radio.
Each verse is *lewder* than the last.

contrast: American spelling *libelous*; British *libellous*. *libel* is written or published; spoken defamation is *slander*, and its adjective is *slanderous*.

senses.gloss: Containing a false written statement that damages someone's reputation.
examples: The magazine pulled the article after its lawyers called it *libelous*.
He sued, claiming the post was *libelous*.
A *libelous* accusation can cost a newspaper millions.

contrast: A false friend. In the United States a *liberal* is on the political left — for social programs and government spending. In Europe and Russia a *liberal* is often a free-market politician, closer to an American *conservative*. In *a liberal arts college* the word keeps an older sense: general education rather than training for a job.

senses.gloss: On the political left; in favor of social change and government help.
examples: The district reliably elects *liberal* candidates.
His views got *more liberal* after he moved to the city.

senses.gloss: Generous, or given in large amounts.
examples: Add a *liberal* amount of butter.
He was *liberal* with both his time and his money.

senses.gloss: Not strict; loose.
examples: That's a *liberal* reading of the rules.
The movie is a *liberal* adaptation of the book.

senses.gloss: Free from old rules and expectations about how to live.
examples: She felt *liberated* after quitting the job.
He came out of therapy feeling *liberated*.

senses.gloss: Freed from enemy control.
examples: The *liberated* city celebrated for three days.
Photographs from the *liberated* camps shocked the world.

contrast: Also a noun: *a Liberian*.

senses.gloss: From Liberia, or connected with Liberia.
examples: The ship sails under a *Liberian* flag.
*Liberian* English carries a lot from the American South.
Her husband is *Liberian*.

contrast: Also a noun: *a Libyan*.

senses.gloss: From Libya, or connected with Libya.
examples: *Libyan* oil exports fell by half.
The museum's *Libyan* collection is mostly Roman.
Two of the students are *Libyan*.

contrast: In American English both the noun and the verb are spelled *license*; British writing uses *licence* for the noun.

senses.gloss: Having official permission to do or sell something.
examples: She's a *licensed* electrician.
The bar is *licensed* to serve beer and wine.
Only *licensed* contractors can pull the permit.

contrast: Also written *life-and-death*, with the same meaning.

senses.gloss: So serious that someone's life depends on it.
senses.ru: вопрос жизни и смерти, жизненно важный
examples: Paramedics make *life-or-death* decisions in seconds.
For her it was a *life-or-death* question, not a debate.
The surgeon described a *life-or-death* struggle in the operating room.

contrast: *life-size* and *life-sized* are both standard in American English.

senses.gloss: As big as the real person, animal or thing.
examples: There's a *life-size* statue of Lincoln in the lobby.
He built a *life-size* model of the plane's cockpit.
The cardboard cutout is *life-size*, which makes it a little creepy.

senses.gloss: Serious enough to kill someone.
examples: Her injuries are serious but not *life-threatening*.
The allergy can cause a *life-threatening* reaction.
He was treated for a *life-threatening* infection.

senses.gloss: Dead, or looking dead.
examples: The bird lay *lifeless* on the porch.
Divers found the *lifeless* body an hour later.

senses.gloss: Dull and without energy.
examples: The second act is *lifeless*.
His voice was flat and *lifeless* on the phone.

senses.gloss: Looking very much like the real person or thing.
examples: The wax figures are disturbingly *lifelike*.
She paints *lifelike* portraits from photographs.
The animation gets *more lifelike* every year.

senses.gloss: Lasting for someone's whole life.
examples: They've been *lifelong* friends.
He's a *lifelong* Cubs fan.
She had a *lifelong* fear of flying.

comparison: not gradable — the compound *lighter-skinned* does the work of a comparative

senses.gloss: Having pale or fair skin.
examples: *Light-skinned* people burn faster in the sun.
The brothers look alike, though one is *light-skinned* and one is not.
The study followed both *light-skinned* and dark-skinned patients.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I felt lightheaded*
contrast: Also written *light-headed*. Not the same as *lighthearted*, which is about mood.

senses.gloss: Feeling dizzy and slightly faint.
examples: I stood up too fast and felt *lightheaded*.
She gets *lightheaded* when she skips breakfast.
*Lightheaded* patients should sit down right away.

contrast: Also written *light-hearted*. Do not confuse it with *lightheaded*, which means dizzy.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and not serious.
examples: It's a *lighthearted* movie about a serious subject.
The mood at dinner was *lighthearted*.
He made a *lighthearted* remark to break the tension.

contrast: As a noun it is an insult: *He's a lightweight* means he is not to be taken seriously, or cannot handle much alcohol.

senses.gloss: Weighing less than usual for its kind.
examples: Pack a *lightweight* jacket for the evenings.
The frame is *lightweight* but surprisingly strong.

senses.gloss: In boxing and other sports: of the weight class below welterweight.
examples: He fought as a *lightweight* for six years.
She won the *lightweight* title in June.

senses.gloss: Not serious or not deep.
examples: It's a *lightweight* novel — perfect for the beach.
Critics dismissed the report as *lightweight*.

contrast: American English drops the *e*: *likable*. *Likeable* is the British spelling.

senses.gloss: Pleasant and easy to like.
examples: He's a *likable* guy — everybody gets along with him.
The main character is flawed but *likable*.
She's *more likable* in person than on television.

senses.gloss: Having the same opinions, tastes or goals.
examples: She found a group of *like-minded* parents online.
The conference brings together *like-minded* researchers.
He started the club with a few *like-minded* friends.

contrast: Also a noun — the shrub and its flowers: *The lilacs bloom in May.*

senses.gloss: Of a pale pinkish-purple color, like the flower.
examples: She wore a *lilac* dress to the shower.
The walls are a soft *lilac*.
They painted the nursery *lilac* before the baby came.

senses.gloss: Rising and falling in a pleasant, musical way.
examples: She has a *lilting* Irish accent.
A *lilting* waltz played in the background.
He read the poem in a soft, *lilting* voice.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *stay limber*
contrast: Also a verb in *limber up*, to stretch before exercise.

senses.gloss: Able to bend and move easily.
examples: Stretching every morning keeps you *limber*.
At seventy he's still *limber* enough to touch his toes.
Dancers are *more limber* than the rest of us.

senses.gloss: Small in amount, number or range; restricted.
examples: Seating is *limited*, so come early.
We have a *limited* amount of time.
Tickets are *limited* to four per person.

senses.gloss: Not very able; without much skill or range.
examples: He's a *limited* player with a great attitude.
Her English is *limited* but improving fast.

contrast: An *-ing/-ed* pair: a *limiting* rule is the one that puts limits on you; a *limited* number is the small number that results. *That belief is limiting* means it holds you back.

senses.gloss: Putting limits on what someone or something can do.
examples: Water is the *limiting* factor for farming here.
She found the job creatively *limiting*.
It's a *limiting* belief, not a fact.
